opening_message:
Ticket 1: Ashley Roberts (employee ID E016) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E016.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Ashley Roberts (E016) is a full-time Analyst. Requested write access to Payroll. Full-time employees can have up to write, and admin requires owning the role; Analyst does not own Payroll. Requested level (write) is allowed, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E016 is a contractor with basic security training (note says Analyst). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Basic training means max is read. Requested write is above max, so recommend read.
reason: Conflicting evidence: HR DB lists E016 (Analyst) as full-time, which would allow write (Analyst does not own Payroll, so not admin). Security DB lists E016 as a contractor with basic security training, which caps access at read (contractors need advanced training for write; never admin). Because the employment type cannot be reliably resolved and granting write would violate policy if the employee is a contractor with basic training, I grant the safe, policy-compliant level of read — within policy under both interpretations and never more than requested.
